sentences.text: She walked it that afternoon.
Stile to ridge, the way the map had it, and it was awful.
The bracken came up past her shoulders in the middle stretch and it did not want her there.
It closed behind her.
It got down her collar.

There was a bank two thirds of the way up that was not marked on the map at all and that she had to go up on her hands, and there was a wet patch in a dip near the middle where her boot went in to the ankle and came out with a noise like a kiss.
It took her an hour and ten minutes.
The bottom path takes twenty.
She did it again on the Thursday, because she had left her jumper at the top.
That was all.
That was the entire reason.

She was cross about the jumper and she went back up the way she knew rather than the way that was sensible, and the second time it took fifty minutes because the bracken in the middle stretch was already bent.
In August her cousins came from the coast, three of them, and she took them up that way because she said it was the fastest route to the view.
That was a lie.
She knew it was a lie when she said it.
She has never entirely worked out why she said it — some part of her wanted them to go that way, and the reason was small and private, exactly as the hare had said it would be.
By the following spring there was a line of flattened green from the stile to the ridge, visible from the road if you knew to look.
By the spring after that there was bare earth showing in it in three places.
The year after that somebody put a plank across the wet part near the middle.
Nobody knows who.
Marisol asked four people and they all assumed it had been there for years.
She is grown up now, and she went back once, in her thirties, on a cold bright day in February when the bracken was down and everything was visible.
The path is a path.
It has a sign at the bottom, on the stile, a small green one with the mileage and a little picture of a boot.
It says 800m, which she thought was a nice touch, or would have been if anyone else had been there to say it to.
She went along the top edge of the wood afterwards, where the bracken thins, and she looked for a long time for a beech with a gap between two roots.
She found several beeches.
She found several gaps.
She was not, in the end, entirely surprised, and she did not stay long, because the light was going and she had a train.
